narrative_idea_gen: A homicide detective, shot dead during a sting gone wrong, haunts his own precinct's evidence room, frantically trying to nudge case files and surveillance photos toward his living partner to identify his killer—but a Prohibition-era grifter's ghost who has owned this building for ninety years keeps redirecting his efforts, stealing his momentum with spectral body-checks and slow, deliberate invasions of his space that make clear she finds his big-cop bravado adorable now that he's just as dead and powerless as she is. Because neither ghost can speak or be heard—only shove pencils off desks, flicker lights, and *touch each other*—their escalating war over the evidence room becomes an elaborate, silent, achingly physical negotiation where every attempt he makes to solve his murder gets derailed by her insistence on showing him, through gesture and proximity and the maddening press of her hand against his chest, that the man who killed him is the same crooked captain whose predecessor killed *her*. The whole disaster is narrated by the ghost of a retired desk sergeant who died of a coronary in the break room last winter and now watches from the doorframe each night, cataloguing with deadpan precision the exact moment the detective's righteous fury starts losing ground to the fact that this woman keeps pinning him against the filing cabinets and he has, unmistakably, stopped resisting.

narrative_beats:
# Seven Scene-Level Beats for *The Evidence Room*

---

## Beat 1: The First Night Dead (Evidence room, after hours)

**Concrete action:** The detective — let's call him the detective throughout, because the narrator does, with faintly mocking formality — wakes up on the evidence room floor without knowing he's dead. He tries to open the door. His hand passes through. He slams a palm on the desk and a single pencil rolls two inches. That is the full extent of his power. He spends what remains of the night in escalating, silent, humiliated fury, trying to move a case file toward the edge of the desk where his living partner might notice it in the morning. He manages a quarter-inch. Then a woman in a cloche hat and paste pearls is leaning against the filing cabinets, watching him with an expression he will later learn to recognize as patience but initially reads as contempt.

**Narrative technique — Narrator-as-audience, establishing the deadpan frame:** The desk sergeant narrator introduces himself not through backstory but through *position*: he is in the doorframe. He has always been in the doorframe. He describes the detective's first night with the flat, itemizing precision of a man who has filled out ten thousand incident reports and now applies that same bureaucratic grammar to the afterlife. ("He tried the door handle at 11:47. His hand went through it at 11:47. He tried it again at 11:48. Results were consistent.") This establishes the comic register — procedural language applied to metaphysical crisis — while simultaneously smuggling in the story's emotional rules: the narrator *notices things*, and his noticing is the reader's only access to a world without dialogue.

**What makes it work for this story:** The pencil is this story's white Pomeranian. It is the metonymic object that encodes the detective's entire situation — enormous will, negligible power — in a single physical fact. Chekhov gave us the dog to show that Gurov wasn't yet seeing Anna as a person. Here, the pencil shows that the detective isn't yet seeing his *condition* clearly. He is still thinking like a living cop: gather evidence, build a case, make an arrest. The pencil's two-inch roll is the distance between that fantasy and his reality. The grifter woman watching from the cabinets is, at this stage, merely an obstacle — an unexplained presence he registers the way Gurov registered Anna: as a category (nuisance, civilian, irrelevant), not a person. Her cloche hat and paste pearls are period details that the narrator logs with the same flat specificity he gives everything else, but they are doing secret work: they are telling us she has been here a very long time.

---

## Beat 2: The First War Over the Case Board (Evidence room, night two)

**Concrete action:** The detective has spent the intervening day watching, helpless, as living officers walk through him, joke over coffee, ignore the pencil. His partner glances at the case file — *his* case file, the sting-gone-wrong — and moves it to a stack. That night, the detective begins again. He has developed a method: sustained concentration lets him slide a photograph a few inches at a time. He is trying to isolate a surveillance photo of the man he believes set him up — a mid-level dealer. He gets the photo halfway across the desk. The grifter picks it up — ghosts can touch what other ghosts have moved — and puts it back. He moves it again. She puts it back. He moves it. She doesn't put it back this time. She puts a *different* photograph on top of it: an older photo, deeper in the file, that he hasn't looked at. It shows a younger version of the precinct captain shaking hands with someone at a fundraiser. He shoves it aside. She retrieves it. This goes on for hours. At one point she body-checks him — a full spectral shoulder into his ribs — and he stumbles through a filing cabinet and comes out the other side vibrating with a rage he cannot voice.

**Narrative technique — Silent dialogue through object manipulation:** This is where the story's central formal constraint becomes its engine. Because neither ghost can speak or be heard by the living, every idea must be *enacted* through the movement of physical objects or the movement of bodies. The grifter is trying to tell the detective something — that his killer is not who he thinks — but her only language is *which photograph she picks up*. This creates a form of dramatic irony structurally identical to Chekhov's Beat 2: the reader can see that she is presenting crucial evidence, but the detective, locked in his own investigative script, reads her actions as sabotage. The narrator catalogues the back-and-forth with the exhausted precision of a man scoring a tennis match he didn't ask to watch.

**What makes it work for this story:** The object-manipulation conceit solves a problem that most ghost stories fumble: how to create genuine, escalating conflict between characters who cannot speak. By making the evidence room a shared workspace and the case files a contested text, every repositioned photograph becomes a line of dialogue, every shoved folder an argument. The body-check is the first moment of physical contact between the two ghosts, and the narrator flags it — not sentimentally, but with the notation of a man who has seen enough precinct scuffles to recognize the difference between a hit meant to injure and a hit meant to *get someone's attention*. The reader is meant to feel, beneath the comedy of two dead people fighting over a desk, the faintest tremor of a different kind of story beginning.

---

## Beat 3: The Captain Walks Through Her (Evidence room, day-to-night transition)

**Concrete action:** During the day shift, the precinct captain — living, confident, authoritative — enters the evidence room to pull a file. On his way out, he walks directly through the grifter. She does not flinch. She does not move. But something happens that the narrator describes with unusual care: a stillness comes over her that is different from her usual studied composure. It is the stillness of someone being *walked through by a specific person*, and it tells the narrator — and through him, the reader — that this is not the first time. That night, the grifter does something she has not done before: instead of fighting the detective for the photographs, she sits on the floor beside the filing cabinet labeled 1931–1935 and presses her palm flat against the drawer. She cannot open it. She does not have enough force. She looks at the detective. He has enough force — barely — for a photograph, maybe a folder. A drawer is beyond him. But together, concentrating, they manage to slide it open three inches. Inside: a case file from 1933. A dead woman. A grifter. Cause of death: fall from a window. Investigating officer: the captain's predecessor.

**Narrative technique — Collaborative action as intimacy, combined with the contrapuntal object:** The file drawer is this story's watermelon. It is the object that changes the emotional physics of the scene by introducing a physical task that requires *cooperation*. Up to now, the ghosts have been adversaries fighting over the same objects. The moment they push together — two sets of dead hands on the same metal drawer — is the first act of joint effort, and the narrator notes the mechanical fact of it (the drawer moves three inches; the sound, to living ears, would be almost nothing; a night janitor might blame the building settling) while the reader feels the emotional fact: they touched on purpose, toward a shared goal, and neither pulled away. The 1933 case file is the contrapuntal revelation — it reframes the grifter from obstacle to *victim*, and reframes the detective's murder from an isolated incident to the latest entry in a ninety-year pattern of institutional violence.

**What makes it work for this story:** This is the scene that cracks the detective's investigative frame. He has been treating his death as a case — a solvable problem with a perpetrator and a motive. The 1933 file tells him it is not a case. It is a *tradition*. The captain who walks through the grifter without knowing she is there is the grandson (or spiritual heir) of the man who threw her out of a window, and the precinct that employs them all is the murder weapon. The grifter's patience — her ninety years of haunting this room, waiting for someone who might finally be forced to *look* — is the emotional revelation. The detective is not the protagonist of a thriller. He is the latest person to be killed by the same building he served. The narrator, who died of a coronary in this building's break room, registers this with the quiet of a man who already knew.

---

## Beat 4: The Detective's False Solution (Evidence room, several nights later)

**Concrete action:** The detective, galvanized by the 1933 file, throws himself into the case with renewed fury. He works every night. He has gotten better at moving objects — practice, or maybe rage, amplifies the signal. He isolates a chain of evidence: the current captain's signature on a falsified informant report, a pattern of stings that conveniently eliminated rivals to a specific drug network, and his own name on the operational order that sent him into the ambush. He arranges it all on the desk in a sequence his living partner will recognize. He is proud. He is electric. He is, for the first time since dying, *hopeful*. He positions the final document and turns to the grifter, expecting — what? Gratitude? Acknowledgment? She is standing by the window, not looking at the desk. She is looking at *him*. And her expression, which the narrator describes with the first and only extended passage of something approaching tenderness in the story, is the expression of someone watching a person arrive at an answer that is correct but completely insufficient.

**Narrative technique — The fulfilled genre expectation as emotional hinge:** This mirrors Chekhov's Beat 4 exactly. The detective has completed the plot he thought he was in. He has solved his murder. The evidence is assembled. If this were a crime story, the partner would find the documents, the captain would be arrested, and the detective's ghost would dissipate in peace. Chekhov let the adultery plot *end* at the station — and then kept going. Here, the murder plot is *solved* at the desk — and the story keeps going. Because the grifter's expression tells us, and tells the detective, that identifying your killer is not the same as understanding what happened to you. Justice, in this building, has never arrived by evidence on a desk. The narrator marks this as the night the detective stopped moving for approximately forty-five minutes and simply stood in the middle of the room, which is, the narrator notes, the longest he has been still since dying.

**What makes it work for this story:** The false solution is structurally essential because it honors the detective's competence — he *is* a good cop; he *did* solve the case — while revealing the limits of competence as a response to systemic betrayal. The grifter has been trying to show him not whodunit but *what it means*, and meaning is not something you can arrange on a desk for a living person to find. This is where the genre betrayal begins to bite: the reader came for a ghost-solves-his-own-murder story and is now being asked to stay for something harder and less resolved. The grifter's look — patient, knowing, almost gentle — is the first moment where the detective sees her fully as a person rather than as an obstacle or an ally, and the narrator clocks the shift with the precision of a man who has watched a lot of people realize they are outmatched.

---

## Beat 5: The Night He Stops Working (Evidence room, the following week)

**Concrete action:** The living partner finds the documents. There is a flurry of daytime activity the detective watches helplessly: meetings, phone calls, a visit from Internal Affairs. Then — nothing. The documents are "logged." The investigation is "ongoing." The captain is still in his office. Weeks pass. The IA file is transferred. Transferred again. The detective watches the bureaucratic absorption of his murder in real time and cannot scream. One night, he enters the evidence room and does not go to the desk. He goes to the filing cabinet, sits on the floor beside it, and puts his head in his hands. The grifter sits down next to him. Not touching. Close enough to touch. They stay that way for a long time. Then she reaches over and places her hand on the back of his neck.

**Narrative technique — Silence as the primary dramatic medium, with the narrator's restraint performing the emotion:** This is the scene where the story's formal constraint — no speech, no audibility, only objects and touch — transforms from limitation into expressive power. The grifter's hand on his neck is the most eloquent line of dialogue in the story, and it is not a line at all. The narrator describes the physical fact: her hand, his neck, the duration. He does *not* describe what it means. This is Chekhov's objective method pushed to its structural extreme: because the narrator is a retired desk sergeant and not a poet, his refusal to interpret the gesture feels like characterization, but it also creates the same emotional gap Chekhov exploits with the watermelon. The reader supplies the feeling precisely because no one on the page articulates it. The narrator notes only that the detective did not move her hand. He notes it the way he would note an irregularity in a logbook. The understatement is what makes it devastating.

**What makes it work for this story:** This is the sturgeon moment. The detective has tried to communicate his most important truth — the identity of his killer, the corruption of his captain — to the living world, and the living world has replied with bureaucratic procedure. The gap between his urgency and the system's indifference is the same gap between Gurov's confession and the friend's comment about fish. But here the gap produces not isolation but *connection*: the one person who understands what it means to be killed by this building and ignored by its machinery is sitting next to him on the floor. The grifter's ninety years of experience with institutional erasure is not backstory — it is *expertise*, and what she is offering, with her hand on his neck, is not romance but the companionship of someone who has already survived the specific despair he is entering. The narrator, who died in this building of natural causes and was mourned for exactly one shift and a card from HR, understands this dynamic from a third angle he does not explain.

---

## Beat 6: The Filing-Cabinet Confrontation (Evidence room, deep night)

**Concrete action:** The living world has failed. The captain is still captain. The case is cold. The detective has not worked the evidence in days. But on this night, the grifter takes him by the wrist — the first time she has initiated full, deliberate, purposeful contact — and pulls him to the 1931–1935 cabinet. She has been marshaling her energy. Together, over hours, they open drawer after drawer. They find not just her file but six others: deaths attributed to accidents, suicides, line-of-duty casualties, all connected to informants or small-time criminals who got in the way of the same network the captain's predecessor protected. The grifter lays them out on the floor in a pattern — a timeline. She positions his file at the end of the row. Then she stands in front of him — close, too close, her hand flat against his chest — and does not move. The narrator describes the detective's face with, for the first and only time, a simile: "He looked the way rookies look when they find out the building they work in has been lying to
narrative_story:
# The Evidence Room

## I.

I was in the doorframe. I am usually in the doorframe. Thirty-one years behind the front desk will do that to a man — you learn where to stand so you can see the bullpen, the hallway, and whoever's coming through the door with blood on their shirt at four in the morning, and after a while the posture outlasts the body. My body gave out in the break room on a Tuesday in 2011. Massive coronary. They found me with a coffee mug still in my hand, which I would have appreciated as an image if I'd had any say in it. HR sent a card. Thompson from Narcotics ate the last of my pistachios from the desk drawer before the end of shift. I don't hold it against him. You get hungry on nights.

The detective died on a Friday. Gunshot, close range, in a parking structure off Vine during what the official report would later describe as an "operation with an adverse outcome," which is how the department says a man bled out behind a concrete pillar while his backup was staged three blocks away at a location no one can quite explain authorizing. His body was found by a parking attendant. His badge was already bagged and in the evidence room by the time he woke up on its floor at 11:43 p.m., which I know because I was in the doorframe and I have always been precise about time. You do ten thousand incident logs, you develop the habit. The habit develops you.

He opened his eyes at 11:43. He touched his chest at 11:44, feeling for the wound, and found his shirt intact and dry because the dead don't carry the mess with them, only the memory of it, and even that fades. He stood. He oriented himself. He recognized the room — the filing cabinets, the long desk, the evidence boxes on their labeled shelves — because he'd spent eight years signing things in and out of this room and knew its geography the way a priest knows his church, which is to say with familiarity and a bottomless, unexamined faith that the building was on his side.

He tried the door handle at 11:47. His hand went through it at 11:47. He tried it again at 11:48. Results were consistent.

He tried the wall. He tried bracing his shoulder against the door like they teach you at the academy, which might have worked had the shoulder been in any meaningful way corporeal. He slammed his palm on the desk, which was the first useful thing he did all night, because the desk is real and has been in this room since before the building was renovated in 1974, and old objects hold their sympathy for the dead a little longer than new ones. A pencil rolled two inches. He stared at it. He slammed the desk again. The pencil did not move. He tried the door. His hand went through.

I will not catalogue the full sequence of attempts because there were thirty-seven of them and they were, with minor positional variation, identical. What is worth noting is the quality of his silence. A living person, locked in a room, will swear, yell, kick things, call for help. A dead person cannot produce sound. Air does not cooperate. The vocal cords are a memory of vocal cords. The detective discovered this at approximately 12:15 a.m. when he opened his mouth to shout and nothing came out, and the look on his face was a look I have seen before — not often, but enough. It is the look of someone understanding a large thing all at once and rejecting the understanding completely.

By 1:00 a.m. he had moved past panic into method. This is, I should note, fast. I've watched some of them take weeks. The detective was, whatever else you might say about him, good at his job, and part of being good at his job was an ability to set aside what he was feeling in order to deal with what was in front of him. What was in front of him was a case file — his case file, the sting operation, the adverse outcome — sitting on the desk where a clerk had left it. His plan, as best I could reconstruct it from his movements, was simple: push the file to the edge of the desk where his partner, who came in every morning at 7:15 and set his coffee on the right corner, would have to notice it. Would have to pick it up. Would have to see.

He pushed the file. It moved a quarter-inch. He pushed again. Nothing. Again. Nothing. Again. An eighth of an inch, maybe. It took him forty minutes to confirm what I could have told him in the first five seconds of his death: his full exertion, concentrated into his fingertips, applied with the whole force of his considerable will, was worth about a quarter-inch per effort, with diminishing returns and a refractory period of several minutes during which he could move nothing at all.

He was still pushing at 3:00 a.m. The file had traveled, in aggregate, slightly less than two inches. His face had settled into an expression I recognized from stakeout reports: a fixed, voluntary blankness meant to contain something underneath that would be inconvenient to express. In his case, I believe it was fury. Not fear, not grief — fury, specifically, at the inadequacy of his means relative to his intention. He had always been a man of considerable physical resource. Six-one, two-ten, competitive handball player, once subdued a PCP suspect alone in a Denny's bathroom. Now he could not move a manila folder across a desk.

This is when the woman appeared.

I say appeared, but that isn't right. She'd been there for some time — since before him, since before me, since before the building's last three renovations and the deaths of everyone who remembered her face. She leaned against the filing cabinets along the far wall with the particular ease of someone who has leaned against those specific cabinets for ninety years and has outlasted the joke of it. She wore a cloche hat, cream-colored, slightly crushed on the left side, and a double strand of paste pearls over a drop-waist dress that had been fashionable in the year she died and was now a costume she couldn't take off. Her shoes were T-straps with a modest heel. I am noting these details because I always note details and because they are doing work the detective did not, at this point, recognize: they were telling him she had been dead for a very long time.

He noticed her at 3:22 a.m. He startled. She did not. He looked at her the way you look at a civilian in a crime scene — with brief, categorizing dismissal. She was not a cop. She was not his partner. She was not relevant to his situation. He went back to pushing the file.

She watched him. Her expression, which I had come to know over the years as patience — the unfathomable, architectural patience of someone who has waited through decades for something she has never precisely defined — he read as contempt. He was wrong, but it would take him some time to be wrong usefully.

He pushed the file. A quarter-inch. He rested. He pushed again.

She watched from the filing cabinets without moving, her hands folded over her clutch purse, and if I had been a man who speculated about the inner lives of others, I might have said she was deciding something. But I am not that man. I am a desk sergeant. I report what I see.

She stayed until nearly dawn, and then the light shifted, and she moved to her spot behind the cabinet where the morning couldn't bother her, and the detective stood alone in the middle of the room with two inches of progress and fourteen hours until anyone who could read his evidence would walk through his body on their way to the coffeepot.

---

## II.

The day shift arrived at 6:48 a.m. with Gutierrez from Property first through the door, then two uniforms pulling overtime on a robbery-homicide inventory, then — at 7:15, exactly on schedule, coffee in the right hand — the partner. Detective Marsh. A competent man with narrow shoulders and a habit of reading case files while eating an everything bagel, which meant most of the active folders in this room had a small crescent of cream cheese on their left margins. I had filed a maintenance complaint about this in 2009. It was not acted upon.

The detective positioned himself directly in front of Marsh. He waved. He shouted — or performed the motions of shouting, which is, to be frank, a worse thing to watch than shouting itself because the effort is visible and the effect is nothing. Marsh walked through him on his way to the desk, and the detective experienced for the first time what I can only describe as the specific indignity of being traversed: the momentary sensation of someone else's warmth passing through the space where your organs used to be, followed by the cold that comes after, which is not temperature exactly but the knowledge that you are not an obstacle.

Marsh noticed the case file. The detective went still with an intensity I could feel from the doorframe. Marsh picked it up, glanced at the label — the detective's name, the case number, the date that was also the date of the detective's death — and his face did something complicated and small that involved his jaw tightening and his eyes going to the window and then coming back. He set the file on a stack to his left. The stack was labeled PENDING REVIEW, which I knew from three decades of observation was the stack where files went to die, where PENDING meant INDEFINITE and REVIEW meant NO ONE.

The detective watched this happen.

He watched it the way I imagine a surgeon would watch someone bandage a wound with newspaper. With the kind of restraint that is, itself, a form of violence directed inward.

The day passed. Officers came and went. Phones rang in the bullpen. At one point, the captain — and I will get to the captain, because the captain is where this story lives, but not yet — walked through the evidence room on his way to Records and passed within four inches of the detective, who stood rigid beside the desk like a man at his own funeral, which, I suppose, he was. The captain did not pause. A living person does not pause for what a living person cannot see.

At 6:00 p.m. the day shift left. At 8:00 p.m. the janitor came through. At 9:30 p.m. the building went quiet in the way that only a building full of the living can go quiet — which is to say, it did not go quiet at all. The heating system ticked. The fluorescents in the hallway buzzed on their timers. A pipe somewhere in the walls made the sound pipes make when they are old and have not been replaced because the budget went to overtime.

At 10:00 p.m. the detective began again.

He had developed a method. I could see it in the way he approached the desk — not with the panicked, diffuse effort of the previous night, but with something targeted, almost surgical. He had noticed, as I had noticed decades earlier, that sustained concentration produced incrementally better results than repeated bursts. You did not slam the desk. You placed your hand on the object and you held your intention in your mind like a single note and you let the note sustain until the object moved or you couldn't hold it any longer. It was, in principle, not unlike the breathing exercises they taught at the academy for marksmanship, and the detective, who had qualified expert every year for eight years, took to it naturally.

He was not going for the file this time. He was going for a photograph.

The case file — the sting, the parking structure, the adverse outcome — contained seventeen photographs. Surveillance images, mostly. Cars, license plates, a grainy shot of a motel room doorway. The detective paged through them with excruciating care, each page-turn a thirty-second act of concentration, until he found the one he wanted: a man in a dark jacket crossing a street, face half-turned toward the camera. Miguel Reyes. Mid-level dealer. The man the detective believed had set him up, had fed the bad intel, had drawn him into the parking structure where someone who was not Reyes was waiting with a .40 caliber and a very clear sightline.

He slid the photograph out of the file. It moved. Not easily, not quickly, but it moved — out of the folder, across the desk, toward the edge where Marsh would set his coffee. The detective's face was the face of a man threading a needle in an earthquake. Every inch was a decision. Every inch cost him something I don't have a procedural term for, though if pressed I would call it what the living call *himself*.

The photograph was halfway across the desk when the grifter picked it up.

I should be precise about this, because the mechanics matter: ghosts can touch what other ghosts have moved. This is a rule I did not set and cannot explain. A living person's coffee mug is untouchable — you'll pass through it the way you pass through doors and people and everything else the world has decided you no longer get to hold. But an object that another ghost has displaced enters a kind of liminal state, halfway between the living world and ours, and in that state it can be grasped, lifted, repositioned. The grifter knew this. She had known it for ninety years. She picked up the photograph of Miguel Reyes with the easy authority of a woman accustomed to taking things off tables — wallets, watches, matchbooks, the small liftable wealth of men who were looking at her neckline and not at her hands — and she put it back where it had been.

The detective turned to face her.

What passed between them was not language. It could not be language. But it had the structure of language — a volley, a return, a meaning aimed at and possibly missed. He looked at her. She looked at him. He turned back to the desk and moved the photograph again. She put it back. He moved it. She put it back. He moved it. She —

She did not put it back.

She put a different photograph on top of it.

The detective stared. The photograph she had chosen was older — not surveillance footage but a formal image, clipped from a newspaper or a department newsletter, slightly yellowed at the edges. It showed two men shaking hands at what appeared to be a fundraiser or a civic dinner: white tablecloths, a podium in the background, a banner too blurred to read. One of the men was a city councilman whose name I do not recall. The other was a younger version of the precinct captain — not the current captain, but close enough. The same jaw. The same posture. A family resemblance or an institutional one. The photograph was dated 1987 and it had been filed, by someone with either meticulous habits or a sense of irony, in a subsection of the case folder labeled BACKGROUND / NOT RELEVANT TO PRIMARY INVESTIGATION.

The detective shoved it aside. He did not shove it the way he moved other objects — with deliberation and breath and the sustained-note technique he had taught himself. He shoved it with the flat contempt of a man who has been interrupted while doing real work by someone offering him trivia. It cost him. The effort drained whatever reserve he'd built, and the Reyes photograph stayed where the grifter had buried it under the 1987 image, and by the time he could muster the concentration to try again, she had already retrieved the fundraiser photo and placed it on the desk precisely where he had been positioning his evidence.

He moved it. She replaced it.

He moved it. She replaced it.

The fourth time, he reached for the photograph and she body-checked him — a full spectral shoulder driven into his ribs with the economical force of someone who understands leverage and has been in rooms with men who are bigger than her for the entirety of her life and afterlife. He stumbled sideways, not because the impact was especially strong but because he was not expecting it, and his momentum carried him through the filing cabinet along the east wall. He passed through metal, through folders, through the accumulated paper of nine decades of institutional record-keeping, and emerged on the other side vibrating with a fury so entire and so silent that the fluorescent light above the desk flickered once — which may have been him, or may have been the wiring, and I am not in a position to say which.

He stood there, inside the wall to his elbows, and looked at her.

She stood at the desk with one hand on the fundraiser photograph and the other at her side, and looked at him.

I noted the time. I noted the duration. I noted that the physical contact — her shoulder, his ribs — was the first such contact between them and that it was, in my assessment, consistent not with an intent to injure but with an intent to redirect. I have seen enough precinct scuffles to know the difference. A hit that means *stay down* lands different from a hit that means *look at me*. This was the second kind. He did not know this yet.

He extracted himself from the wall. He went back to the desk. He moved the fundraiser photo aside — slowly this time, not with contempt but with the

Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets.
